newsitem.title: USA: Clinton taps FCC lawyer to be agency's new chairman.
newsitem.headline: Clinton taps FCC lawyer to be agency's new chairman.

text.p: President Clinton on Wednesday tapped the Federal Communications Commission's top lawyer to be its new chairman at a time when the agency faces sweeping changes and huge challenges in the communications business.

William Kennard, a Democrat, has been the FCC's general counsel for 3-1/2 years. If, as expected, he wins Senate confirmation, Kennard, 40, would be the first black to head the five-member regulatory agency.

Clinton also nominated Michael Powell, age 34 and the son of former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Colin Powell, to be a member of the FCC, which oversees the telephone, broadcasting, wireless communications, cable TV and satellite industries.
Powell, the chief of staff of the Justice Department's antitrust division, would fill a Republican vacancy.

Clinton is in the process of filling four vacancies at the FCC, giving him the opportunity to influence the agency's decisions on matters ranging from liquor advertising on television to free TV air time for political candidates.
Kennard would replace Reed Hundt, who plans to resign as chairman after a controversial 3-1/2 year tenure in which he oversaw implementation of last year's telcommunications reform act.

Many of the FCC's key rules are being challenged in court. The $100 billion local phone market remains a monopoly dominated by the regional Baby Bells and GTE Corp., despite the new telecommunications law. At the same time, mergers are sweeping through the phone and broadcast industires.
Kennard is "taking the reins at a time when there's just more turbulence than ever before," said Jeffrey Kagan, of Kagan Telecom Associates in Atlanta.

Clinton also is expected to nominate Gloria Tristani, 43, an elected member of the New Mexico State Corporation Commission, to a Democratic vacancy on the FCC. The state commission oversees the phone and insurance industries.
Those who know Kennard say he is a consensus builder and well-versed in the communications industry.
"He will advance competition and do so by creating a consensus among industry players," said Scott Harris, a lawyer with Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher and a former FCC official.

Kennard's personable style also is expected to allow him to win over fellow commissioners. Hundt deadlocked with other commissioners on issues such as broadcast liquor ads and the public-service obligations of TV stations in the digital age.
"It will be easier for Bill to build consensus and get majorities," said attorney Alfred Mamlet of Steptoe & Johnson.
The new commissioners will have their hands full.
"Clearly, one of the FCC's biggest challenges ahead is to crack open the local phone market. It's not open today," said Mamlet.

Critics complain that last year's sweeping communications act has done little to jump-start competition in local phone service. A portion of the FCC's landmark ruling to open up the local market to new rivals, including long distance phone companies, was recently thrown out by a U.S. appeals court.
While he is well-regarded, Kennard's nomination may face bumpy sailing in the Senate.

His selection already has stirred the ire of Sen. Ernest Hollings of South Carolina, the top Democrat on the Commerce Committee, which must clear any FCC nomination. Hollings had pushed for Ralph Everett, a former top staffer on the commerce panel and now a Washington attorney.
But Kennard is expected to win confirmation.
Clinton already has nominated Harold Furchtgott-Roth, chief economist for the House Commerce Committee, to fill a Republican vacancy.
Neither of the two major political parties can control more than three of the five seats at the FCC.
